newsitem.title: JAPAN: Lower prices unlikely to spark gold rush in Japan.
newsitem.headline: Lower prices unlikely to spark gold rush in Japan.

text.p: Falling bullion prices and a rising yen have cut retail gold prices in Japan but consumers, among the most avid gold buyers in the world, are not expected to take advantage of the situation to create a "gold rush".

"Physical buying of gold has risen slightly since early July when yen-based retail prices began falling," said Makoto Tonoki, general manager of Tanaka Kikinzoku Jewelry KK, a unit of a major bullion house.

"But it is far from a 'gold boom'. I think the price levels are not attractive enough for investors to step up gold buying considering we saw yen-based retail prices sag below 1,100 yen ($9) in 1995," he said.

Dollar-based gold prices slumped to fresh 12-year lows of below $320 on Monday after the Reserve Bank of Australia said late last week it had sold two-thirds of its gold reserves, or 167 tonnes, over the previous six months.
Precious metal industry sources said investors are waiting for yen-based gold retail prices to dip further before buying amid bearish sentiment towards gold.

Cheaper bullion prices, combined with the yen's firmer tone, have helped to push down yen-based gold retail prices. Gold was quoted at 1,202 yen per gram retail on Tuesday, down from this year's high of 1,467 yen on April 10, but higher than the 20-year low of 1,070 yen marked on May 1995.
"Large-scale buying (about 50 kg) has not been detected. Major investors are waiting for prices to go down further, say, to around 1,150 yen," another senior official of a major bullion house said.
Precious metal industry sources said Japan's gold imports for June are likely to remain low, probably below nine tonnes, but added that gold imports could recover to above 10 tonnes in July.
In addition to current prices, moves by central banks around the world to dispose of their gold holdings are seen as a negative factor for gold investment in Japan.

"Investors may be discouraged from buying gold in the wake of Australia's decision to sell gold, which suggests a change in gold holding policies around the world," one precious metal industry source said.

Enthusiasm for gold has been crumbling over the past few months. Central banks in the Netherlands and Belgium have sold part of their gold reserves, and the U.S. Federal Reserve has recently issued a paper suggesting central banks have no need to hold gold.

Despite recent remarks by Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto that Japan had in the past been tempted to sell U.S. Treasuries and boost its gold reserves, industry sources said chances were slim that Japan would increase its gold reserves.
Cumulative gold imports by Japan in the first five months of 1997 totalled 59.59 tonnes, down from 66.14 tonnes in the same period a year earlier, according to Finance Ministry data. ($1=113 yen)
